title: The ideal LBO candidate
objectives: Answer out loud: What makes a good LBO candidate?

blocks.body:
- Stable, predictable cash flow (to service debt)
- Low CapEx needs (more cash for debt paydown)
- Strong market position and defensible moat
- Tangible assets for collateral
- Room for operational improvement or cost cuts
- Strong management team
- Clear exit path (strategic buyers or IPO)
- Reasonable purchase price

blocks.title: What makes a bad LBO candidate?
blocks.teaser: Highly cyclical revenue, heavy CapEx, rapid technological disruption, negative or volatile cash flow, or a business that depends on constant reinvest…
blocks.body:
Highly cyclical revenue, heavy CapEx, rapid technological disruption, negative or volatile cash flow, or a business that depends on constant reinvestment (early-stage tech). All of these struggle to service fixed debt.

**Interview answer:** "Volatile or cyclical cash flow and heavy CapEx, since the business has to reliably pay interest and debt."

blocks.prompt: Which company is the WORST LBO candidate?

options.text: A subscription software company with 95% retention
A highly cyclical manufacturer with heavy CapEx
A market-leading distributor with stable margins
A services business with low CapEx and recurring contracts

blocks.explanation: Volatile, cyclical cash flow and heavy CapEx make it hard to reliably service fixed debt.

blocks.title: Why do PE firms like recurring revenue?
blocks.teaser: It makes cash flow predictable, which lets the company carry more debt safely.
blocks.body: It makes cash flow predictable, which lets the company carry more debt safely.
